title: WHO SINNED?
paragraphs: WHO SINNED?
That was the question echoing in the dust.

A man sat beside the road—
eyes open…
but never seeing.

Born blind.
Born into whispers.
Born into blame.
People didn’t see a man.
They saw a theological problem.

“Rabbi,” the disciples asked Jesus,
“who sinned—this man or his parents—that he was born blind?”
— Gospel of John 9:2
Translation:
Someone must be guilty.

Because suffering makes us uncomfortable.
We want a culprit.

A mistake.
A curse.
A scandal.
But Jesus flipped the question.
Not Who sinned?
But What if God is about to move?

“Neither this man nor his parents sinned,” Jesus said,
“but this happened so that the works of God might be displayed in him.”
— Gospel of John 9:3
Pause there.
The man’s blindness was not the final sentence.
It was the stage.
Then Jesus did something strange.
He spat on the ground.

Mud.
Dust.
Clay in His hands.
The same hands that once formed Adam from the earth.
Jesus pressed the mud onto blind eyes.
“Go wash in the Pool of Siloam.”
The man obeyed.
And for the first time in his life—
Light.

Colors.
Faces.
Sky.
The world exploded into sight.
But here’s the twist nobody expected.
The miracle didn’t end the controversy.
It started one.
The religious leaders interrogated him.
“How were your eyes opened?”
They weren’t celebrating the miracle.
They were defending their system.

And the healed man—
once a silent beggar—
became a bold witness.

“I was blind,” he said.
“Now I see.”
That sentence has echoed through centuries.
Because it’s more than eyesight.
It’s the Gospel.
Every one of us starts the same way.
Not physically blind.
But spiritually.
The Bible says sin darkens the heart.

We stumble through life guessing…
groping…
blaming…
Until Jesus touches our eyes.
Christ is not just a teacher.
He is the Light of the World.
That’s exactly what Jesus said earlier in the same chapter.

“I am the light of the world.”
— Gospel of John 9:5
When His light enters your life, something radical happens.
You begin to see:

• Your sin clearly
• God’s holiness clearly
• And the cross of Christ clearly
Because the greatest blindness is not in the eyes.
It’s in the heart.
And the greatest miracle is not restored vision.
It’s redemption.
Jesus went to the cross so blind sinners like us could finally see.

Forgiven.
Washed.
Made new.
Friend, maybe people have labeled you.

Your past.
Your mistakes.
Your family.

Maybe the world keeps asking,
“Who sinned?”
But Jesus asks a different question:
“Do you want to see?”
And if you come to Him—
Really come—
Your story can become the same as that once-blind man.
“I was blind.
But now I see.”
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
